https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: ‘We are deeply saddened’ … Nathan Trevallion and Catherine Birmingham were raising their three children off-grid in Italy View image in fullscreen ‘We are deeply saddened’ … Nathan Trevallion and Catherine Birmingham were raising their three children off-grid in Italy Italy Off-grid UK-Australian couple describe ‘anguish’ at removal of children by Italian court After judge allows partial access rights, Catherine Birmingham and Nathan Trevallion say the enforced separation ‘broke each of our hearts’ Tory Shepherd Thu 3 Sep 2026 06.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A couple have told of their heartache, trauma and stress after fighting for two years for their right to parent their children as they choose in the glare of the world’s attention . The three children of a Melbourne woman, Catherine Birmingham, and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, were removed from their “ dilapidated ” off-grid home in Italy last year. It sparked global conversations about state intervention and alternative lifestyles. They were raising the children on a property in the woods in the Abruzzo region, where they grew their own food and homeschooled the children. Off-grid UK-Australian couple given more access to children who were removed from home in Italy Read more In September 2024, the family was hospitalised after eating poisonous mushrooms they had picked, which brought them to the attention of authorities. In November 2025, the juvenile court ordered the removal of Utopia Rose, nine, and six-year-old twins Galorian and Bluebell to a residential care facility, citing a lack of hygiene, social interaction, toilet facilities and schooling. Birmingham stayed with them until March, when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling. On Wednesday, an Italian court approved a staged process that would allow a “ gradual reunification process ”, and could eventually allow the children to leave the facility. “The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a ‌gradual reunification process, ‌allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend ‌overnight stays with their family,” their lawyer, Simone Pillon, said . In a statement released on Thursday, the couple said the “long-awaited decision, which our entire family awaited with anguish, arrived with a harshness that broke each of our hearts”. They asked whether forcing school attendance was “fair, legal, and respectful” of their parental rights and the rights of their children, saying they chose Italy for reasons including its homeschooling rights and support for family bonds. The parents have said that doctors say the children’s health is at “serious risk” and “the only way to reduce this risk is to return them home immediately”. “We are deeply concerned for their health,” the parents wrote. “How will they be well if they are forced to travel back and forth from their home to the foster home, then to school, and then back to the foster home again, all while still being kept apart from their parents? “How will they fare in the evening when, after an afternoon spent at home with their friends and pets, they must return to the foster home?” Even Italy’s hard-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has weighed in. She expressed “alarm” over the children being taken into care, while the deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, compared the case to a kidnapping. But the judiciary’s union said the court’s decision was based on factors including the children’s safety, sanitary conditions and education. After the latest decision, social services will monitor the process and make an assessment before any permanent reunion can happen. The couple wrote that the authorities wanted to impose a standard. “And those who don’t follow it lose their children,” they wrote. “We are deeply saddened by this. “We have continued to collaborate and engage with everyone, even under extreme trauma, stress, exasperation and concern for our children knowing their daily suffering but we will always demand respect for our parental rights and, above all, for our children’s rights, especially their right to health – mental, physical and emotional.” The couple plan to appeal for a complete and faster reunification. Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, spoke with the Press Association following meetings with Ed Miliband and Wes Streeting Photograph: The Ditchley Foundation/PA View image in fullscreen Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, spoke with the Press Association following meetings with Ed Miliband and Wes Streeting Photograph: The Ditchley Foundation/PA Nato Nato head: Britain must show ‘credible path’ of annual defence budget increases Mark Rutte said Britain will need to steadily increase defence spending to meet Nato target of 3.5% of GDP by 2035 Dan Sabbagh Thu 17 Sep 2026 15.29 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 16.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Britain needs to show “a credible path” of annual increases in its defence budgets to meet a Nato target of spending nearly £30bn more on the military by the middle of the next decade, the head of the alliance said on Thursday. Mark Rutte, Nato’s secretary general, said that Britain could not wait until just before 2035 to lift defence spending to 3.5% of GDP, in an unusually pointed intervention a day after he met prime minister Andy Burnham . In an interview with the Press Association, he said: “And that is why you need a credible path towards that 3.5%, and yearly increments.” The alliance’s secretary general, a former Dutch prime minister, made similar remarks to the BBC, where he said that the UK understood that the target could not be met “in one go in 2034” and that it would have to be achieved gradually. Earlier on Thursday, Rutte met with Wes Streeting , the defence secretary, and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary. He saw Burnham on Wednesday, at a business park in Didcot, and also met representatives from the defence industry. Keir Starmer signed the UK up to a Nato-wide target of increasing defence spending to 3.5% of GDP in the summer of 2025, under pressure from the US president, Donald Trump. The figure has since been endorsed by Burnham and his chancellor, former defence secretary John Healey. Current spending plans, covering until 2028/9, show defence spending levelling off at 2.7%, nearly £30bn below the ultimate target, raising the question of how it would be achieved after the next general election. It is unclear if taxes or borrowing would have to rise, or other government spending cuts. Healey resigned as defence minister in June because Starmer would not commit to lifting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. At the time Healey said Labour needed to set “a clear path” to meet the Nato commitment, similar language to that used by Rutte in his interviews. But since then Healey and Burnham have avoided committing to the 3% by the end of the decade. Decisions on future spending are likely to be left to the next government spending review due next year, prompting the Nato leader to engage in public lobbying on his trip to Britain. Rutte said he was certain the Burnham government remained behind the ultimate goal and the need to increase defence spending gradually. “I am absolutely confident that when it comes to the yearly increments, they totally take it and accept it, that they have to be there,” he told the BBC. “There has to be a credible path. What that credible path exactly will be, we will see with the spending review next year,” Rutte added. A day earlier, Rutte gave a speech to at Ditchley Park in Oxfordshire , in which he warned that the 32 country military alliance faced “the most dangerous and complex security environment in a generation” with wars in Ukraine, the Middle East coming at time of rising state competition. Nato needed “more UK and more Europe”, he added, to take up the slack as the US reduces its military commitment to the alliance. Trump has long argued that the UK and Europe should match US levels of defence spending and take the lead in defending the continent from Russia aggression. Honour guards then carried the coffin in a state procession to the Church of St Sophia, where crowds queued to pay their respects. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Samuel spent his reign fighting the Byzantine Empire to expand his kingdom, and he died in 1014. His bones were found in a Greek border area 60 years ago, and Bulgaria has negotiated with Athens for decades to bring them home. Saturday's handover follows an agreement this week between the Bulgarian and Greek culture ministers. Under it, Bulgaria will give back religious relics taken from Greek monasteries during the First World War. https://baltic-review.com/riga-industry-.text: Share Tweet 0 Riga’s University of Latvia is hosting a day of presentations, laboratory visits and technology discussions on September 24. From laboratory research to practical cooperation Researchers, technology developers and business representatives are meeting in Riga on Thursday, September 24, for a full-day programme designed to connect scientific work with possible industrial applications. Industry Day and Sensing the Future, organised by the University of Latvia and the university’s Institute of Solid State Physics, combines technology presentations, laboratory visits and discussions about future cooperation. The event is taking place at two University of Latvia locations: the Institute of Solid State Physics in Kengarags during the morning and the University of Latvia House of Science in Torņakalns in the afternoon. The programme is focused on research areas that are already close to commercial use or could support new products and services. According to the event organisers, the day is intended to give companies a clearer view of technologies being developed in Latvia while allowing researchers to receive feedback from potential users. The format is therefore less about a conventional academic conference and more about creating direct contacts between laboratories, companies and innovation networks. Two research projects in the morning programme The morning Industry Day programme includes presentations on the FeLow-D and SWEB projects. FeLow-D is working with functionally low-dimensional ferroelectric materials, which can be relevant to advanced electronic and biomedical devices. The project brings together scientists from several countries and has a budget of €2.5 million. Its potential application areas include electronics, sensors, energy production and medical technologies. Presenting the project to industry audiences allows researchers to discuss not only scientific progress but also questions such as manufacturing, scalability and the needs of possible technology partners. The second featured project, SWEB, is developing smart windows for zero-energy buildings. Its work includes functional coatings, thin-film technologies and methods for applying those coatings at larger scale. The organisers say the technologies could also be relevant to greenhouses, optical products and advanced manufacturing. These examples illustrate a broader direction in Latvia’s research policy: strengthening the path from publicly supported research towards practical use. The event does not promise immediate commercial products, but it creates a setting in which researchers and companies can assess whether further testing, joint development or technology transfer is realistic. Quantum computing and DNA data storage in the afternoon The afternoon programme, titled Sensing the Future, moves to the University of Latvia House of Science. It is being held within the BioPhoT programme and broadens the discussion to technologies shaping future energy systems, communications and advanced manufacturing. The agenda includes a conversation with Professor Koen Bertels on quantum computing, DNA data storage and Unveil models. The programme also features technology presentations, an “Industry Reality Check” and a short matchmaking format intended to help participants identify possible partners quickly. For a research community, such a format can be valuable because commercialisation often depends on contacts outside a single scientific field. A materials researcher may need a manufacturer, while a software developer may need access to specialised laboratory equipment or a test environment. Bringing those groups together in one day can help clarify which ideas are ready for development and which still require basic research. A practical meeting point for Latvia’s innovation ecosystem The event comes as Latvia continues to seek stronger links between universities, research institutes and companies. ResearchLatvia has highlighted research commercialisation and industry collaboration as important parts of the country’s innovation agenda, including through international exchanges focused on how scientific results can be brought closer to the market. Industry Day offers a local, face-to-face version of that objective. Laboratory tours can make research infrastructure more visible to companies, while direct discussion gives scientists an opportunity to understand the technical and business requirements of potential partners. The organisers describe the programme as an opportunity to learn about emerging technologies, exchange views and build new cooperation contacts. Participation is conducted in English, and the event is aimed at researchers, innovators, technology developers and representatives of industry. Rather than presenting science as a finished product, the Riga programme focuses on the intermediate stage where ideas are tested, explained and matched with practical needs. That makes the event relevant not only to established companies but also to start-ups, research teams and organisations looking for new applications in energy efficiency, sensing, biomedicine and digital technologies.
